sections.heading: Dialogue II, Knot ix, part 2 (printed pp. 221–229)
rows: [p. 221] Ereu. Nescio quid respondeam de pondere ex navis arbore deiecto. Imprimis enim experimentum credo esse captu difficile, dum enim passis velis & insigni aliqua celeritate fertur navis, nescio quomodo malus tam rectus staturus sit & inconcussus, ut modica differentia notari possit; deinde ex ea parte mali demittendum est pondus, unde fugit navis; alioquin pondus ab ipso malo prae se agitur; sequitur autem in eo casu malum ingens [p. 222] ventus, qui an permittat experimento locum nescio.

[p. 221] Ereu. I do not know what I should answer about the weight thrown down from the ship’s mast [arbore]. For first of all I believe the experiment to be difficult to grasp [captu difficile]; for while, with sails spread [passis velis] and with some notable [insigni] speed, the ship is borne, I do not know how the mast is to stand so straight and unshaken that a moderate difference can be noted; next, the weight is to be let down from that part of the mast whence [unde] the ship flees; otherwise the weight is driven by the mast itself before it [prae se]; there follows, moreover, in that case, the mast [malum] a huge [p. 222] wind, which, whether it permits place to the experiment, I do not know.

Praeterea videtur Galilaeus putare proiectam sphaeram in superficie horizontali polita, conservaturam impetum in aeternum. Ego vero impressam illam qualitatem nihil Simplicio magis sapio. Sed de eo alias. Nunc hoc indico, tolli velle Galilaeum omne quod est ex medio, impedimentum, quod (si credendum est orationi supra habitae) est medium ipsum tollere, cum e diverso ex resistentia medii motus ipsius limitatio semper desumenda sit.

Besides, Galileo seems to think that a sphere projected on a polished horizontal surface will conserve its impetus for eternity. I, however, savour [sapio] that impressed quality [impressam qualitatem] not a whit more than Simplicio. But of that elsewhere. Now I point out this: that Galileo wishes every impediment that is from the medium [ex medio] to be removed, which (if the discourse [orationi] held above is to be believed) is to remove the medium itself, since, on the contrary [e diverso], the limitation [limitatio] of motion itself is always to be taken from the resistance of the medium [medii].
Andab. Siccine est, Ereuni? cedo itaque in quo medio versetur orbis hic ex tellure confectus & mari, & a quo motus ipsius limitatio desumitur.
Andab. Is it so, Ereunius? Tell [me] [cedo], then, in what medium this orb made up of earth [tellure] and sea is engaged [versetur], and from what the limitation of its motion is taken.

Ereu. Melius postmodum haec explicuissem, sed quoniam nunc urges sic accipe. Non vides undas vento, Tellurem undis resistere? Vides ergo unde ventus & undae vis remittatur, hoc est, unde velocitati motus terminus figatur. Motus enim sine causa & quidem praesentanea nullus est: quantitatem itaque causae qui signat, & motui fines praescribit. Et haec quidem est introrsus limitatio, superficiem autem versus quomodo limitetur in propatulo est. At nunc quomodo institutum cursum repetam, fugit me ratio, adeo in praecipiti me interpolasti.

Ereu. I would have explained these things better afterwards, but since you press now, take [it] thus. Do you not see the waves resist the wind, the Earth [Tellurem] the waves? You see therefore whence the force [vis] of wind and wave is slackened [remittatur], that is, whence a term [terminus] is fixed to the swiftness of the motion. For motion without a cause, and indeed a present [praesentanea] one, is none: he therefore who marks [signat] the quantity of the cause, also prescribes ends to the motion. And this indeed is the limitation inwards [introrsus]; but how it is limited towards the surface is in the open [in propatulo]. But now the way [ratio] in which I should resume the course undertaken [institutum cursum] escapes me, so headlong [in praecipiti] have you broken in upon me [interpolasti].

[p. 223] Andab. Cavebo postmodum: sed & nunc praestabo manum, docebas si quidem nos, quomodo motus ex medii resistentia foret & sublata medii resistentia, nullus futurus foret motus, atque nullus proinde infinitus esse possit sine perpetua causa. [Margin: Experimenta de vi motus communis.] Sed & premunt te plura experimenta quae dicuntur exercita: ut quod pila demissa ab equo concitatissimo, sequatur equi cursum. Audio & sagittam e chiroballista emissam in curru inter currendum visam a circumstantibus spectabili flexu currum sequi. Excussam tubo nitrii pulveris vi pilam, tubo insimul converso motum circularem concipere, & inde fieri, ut aves in medio volatu intercipiantur, inaudivi a tuo Galilaeo proditum, quid ad haec omnia reponis?

[p. 223] Andab. I will beware afterwards: but even now I will lend [praestabo] a hand. You were teaching us, indeed [si quidem], how motion would be from the resistance of the medium, and, the resistance of the medium taken away, there would be going to be [futurus foret] no motion, and accordingly none can be infinite without a perpetual cause. [Margin: Experiments concerning the force of common motion [motus communis].] But several experiments also press you which are said to have been carried out [exercita]: as that a ball let down from a horse urged on most swiftly [concitatissimo] follows the course of the horse. I hear also that an arrow shot from a hand-ballista [chiroballista] in a chariot while running was seen by the bystanders to follow the chariot with a noticeable bending [flexu]. That a ball shot out from a tube by the force of nitre powder, the tube being turned at the same time, conceives a circular motion, and that thence it comes about that birds are intercepted in mid flight, I have heard [inaudivi] given out [proditum] by your Galileo; what do you reply to all these things?

Ereu. Memini iam & sermonem inde exordium sumpsisse quod obiecisset Asphalius demissum ab arbore navali pondus, ab ipsius mali cursu deficere; quod mihi facile confitendum est, modo de experimento constet. Non enim puto contra veritatem quam profitemur, quicquam praestare: cum enim aer circumstans navim proprio motu feratur, diverso a navi, non puto hoc exemplo multum premi Copernicum: neque enim de motu communi procedit, seu de motu per accidens; sed de impressione facta a causa movere desi-[p. 224]stente. Neque si experimentum in contrarium accidat tantillum ipsi proficere crediderim; tot enim circumstant ut in quam causam referendus sit effectus non facile sit {?constitutum} [printed: constiturum].

Ereu. I remember now also that the conversation took its beginning from this, that Asphalius had objected that a weight let down from a ship’s mast [arbore navali] falls short [deficere] of the course of the mast itself; which is easily to be confessed by me, provided that it be established [constet] about the experiment. For I do not think it avails [praestare] anything against the truth which we profess: for since the air standing around the ship is borne with a proper motion, diverse from the ship, I do not think Copernicus is much pressed by this example: for it does not proceed about common motion [motu communi], or about motion by accident [per accidens], but about the impression [impressione] made by a cause ceasing [p. 224] to move. Nor, if the experiment should fall out to the contrary, would I believe it to profit him [ipsi] even a tiny bit [tantillum]; for so many things stand around [circumstant] that to which cause the effect is to be referred would not be easily established.

Quo ad haec modo quae tu obiicis, Andabata, imprimis Galilaeo ne impingas calumniam qui recitat quidem quod de iaculatione in aves volantes dicis; sed idem non constare dicit adiectis sententiae suae firmamentis. De pila sequente cursum praecipitem Equitis, primo experimentum cate & solerter faciendum est, ne qua iactatio interveniat vel pilae, vel brachii equitis; iterum quanto tempore sequatur equitem videndum est: fortassis enim donec aer quieverit, quem equus in ipsa demissione concitat, & tunc alieno parenti assignatus fuerit hic partus. De sagitta ex curru praecipiti emissa testes peto. Sed neque satis intelligo quomodo contingere possit: si enim sagitta ad perpendiculum evolaverit, motus quo sequatur currum a transversa sagitta fiet, qua aerem secare quam incredibile sit experti sciunt, & tantumdem est de iaculo quod Eques excussum manu recepturus sit.

As to these things just now [modo] which you object, Andabata, first of all do not fasten [impingas] a calumny on Galileo, who indeed recites what you say about the shooting [iaculatione] at flying birds; but the same [man] says that it is not established [non constare], with supports [firmamentis] added to his opinion. About the ball following the headlong course of the Horseman, first the experiment is to be made shrewdly [cate] and skilfully, lest any tossing [iactatio] intervene, either of the ball or of the horseman’s arm; again, it is to be seen for how much time it follows the horseman: for perhaps [it follows] until the air has come to rest which the horse stirs up in the very letting-down, and then this offspring [partus] will have been assigned to a parent not its own [alieno parenti]. About the arrow shot from a headlong chariot I ask for witnesses. But neither do I sufficiently understand how it could happen: for if the arrow has flown out to the perpendicular, the motion by which it follows the chariot will be made by the arrow crosswise [a transversa sagitta], in which [position] how incredible it is that it cuts the air, those who have tried [experti] know; and just as much is [to be said] about the javelin which the Horseman is to receive back in his hand after shooting it out [excussum].

Quae autem me retinent ne huic sententiae assentiar, plura sunt. Videmus enim aerem ut levem impetum nanciscatur multum comprimi & condensari, quod in casu motus cum tellure fieri impossibile est: impediret enim caeteros [p. 225] omnes motus. Videntur mihi quoque exempla ordinaria potius obstare quam adiuvare. Cur enim qui arcubus vel ballistis certant quis remotius iaculetur, cur inquam non motu aliquo se concitant? Cur non equis, curribus, navibus insident? si motus horum augent motum sagittarum? Parthi antiquitus, hodie Tartari equites sagittarios habent qui & procurrendo & recurrendo sagittas emittunt: a neutris tamen notatum accepimus, vel breviores esse fugientium vel fortiores accedentium iactus. Hodie nihil notius est quam naves unas alias insequi, dum utraeque tormentis certant. Num fugientium necessum est leviores esse ictus quam insequentium? aut breviori spatio opus est, dum fugiunt, quam dum insequuntur? Nostri certe duces non hoc testantur, neque dum navis subsidit vel elevatur, motum notant, sed situm, ut hostem feriant. Haec omnia cum quotidie & magnis studiis exerceantur, si quis notabilis in motu effectus esset, omnino latere non posset.

But the things which hold me back lest I assent to this opinion are several. For we see that the air, in order that it may obtain a light impetus, is much compressed and condensed, which in the case of motion with the earth [tellure] is impossible to be done: for it would impede all the other [p. 225] motions. The ordinary examples also seem to me rather to stand against than to aid. For why do those who contend with bows or ballistae [over] who may shoot further, why, I say, do they not set themselves going by some motion? Why do they not sit upon horses, chariots, ships? if the motions of these increase the motion of arrows? The Parthians anciently, the Tartars today, have mounted archers [equites sagittarios] who both in running forward and in running back shoot arrows: from neither, however, have we received it [as] noted, either that the shots [iactus] of those fleeing are shorter, or [that those] of those approaching [are] stronger. Today nothing is better known than that ships pursue one another, while both contend with cannon [tormentis]. Is it necessary that the blows [ictus] of those fleeing be lighter than [those] of those pursuing? or is there need of a shorter space while they flee than while they pursue? Our commanders certainly do not attest this, nor, while the ship sinks or is raised, do they note the motion, but the position [situm], that they may strike the enemy. Since all these things are exercised daily and with great zeal, if there were any notable effect in the motion, it could by no means lie hidden.

Asphal. Ergone hoc incusas illud in quo aliud fertur, ei impetum communicare? quod mihi videtur & constanti ratione & perpetuis muniri exemplis. Nam quid evidentius peti possit, quam si ego movear id quod prae me est, a me agi? quid autem aliud est si pilam manu [p. 226] gestem, quam eam prae aliqua mei parte esse, qua illam praeagam? Et si vis exemplis quotidianis rem geri: quid frequentius quam nos dum equo, curru, navi vectamur, si equus territus subito constiterit, vel retrocesserit vel deviaverit, subito concuti, & non praevisi motus sentire effectum? Tantumdem est si currus vel navicula impegerit. Ad saltum, vel etiam lapidis iactum sive manu, sive funda procurri videmus, ut vehementior sit iactus. Addo his pondera graviora maiori impetu ferri. Vide malleos fabrorum inaequales unde musici concentus exordium traxisse feruntur. Et considera quantum malleus gravior tanto maiorem ictum facere; quod, si non toto corpore impetum secum ferret, nunquam accideret. Si solis externis partibus ageret, pares essent plerorumque ictus, sicut & impetus, ut vides.

Asphal. Do you then [Ergone] find fault with [incusas] this: that that in which another thing is borne communicates impetus to it? which seems to me to be fortified both by constant reason and by perpetual examples. For what more evident could be sought than, if I am moved, that that which is before me is driven [agi] by me? and what else is it, if I carry a ball in my hand, [p. 226] than that it is before some part of me by which I drive it before [me] [praeagam]? And if you wish the matter to be conducted by everyday examples: what more frequent than that we, while we are carried [vectamur] by horse, chariot, ship, if the horse, frightened, has suddenly stood still, or has stepped back or turned aside, are suddenly shaken, and feel the effect of an unforeseen motion? Just as much is it if a chariot or a little boat has struck [impegerit]. For a leap, or even for the throw of a stone whether by hand or by sling, we see [men] run forward, that the throw may be more vehement. I add to these that heavier weights are borne with greater impetus. See the unequal hammers of the smiths, from which the musical harmony [concentus] is said to have drawn its beginning. And consider: by how much a hammer is heavier, by so much it makes a greater blow; which, if it did not bear the impetus with itself with its whole body, would never happen. If it acted by the external parts alone, the blows of most [hammers] would be equal, just as also the impetuses [impetus], as you see.

Ereu. Ex re obiecisti, Asphali, & ex re ipsa tibi repono. Si hoc tantum quaeritur ut motus imprimatur, me non repugnantem habes. Sed aliud est motum ex vectatione inesse, aliud impetum, qui ad motum cessante causa concitatum satis sit. Hunc refugio, illum in plerisque ultroneus amplector. Si quid aliud ante se prae agit, motum crediderim aequalem imprimere: Video enim quod manu gestatur quasi unum cum ipsa manu esse, & per a-[p. 227]liud moveri. Certe si sensus consulendus sit in navi aequaliter ad horizontem cursu quantumvis citatissimo expulsa, magis ventum, quam navis motum sentimus.

Ereu. You have objected from the matter [Ex re], Asphalius, and from the matter itself I reply to you. If this only is asked, that motion be impressed, you have me not resisting. But it is one thing for motion to be in [a thing] from carriage [ex vectatione], another for impetus [to be in it] which may suffice for the motion excited [concitatum], the cause ceasing. This [latter] I shrink from [refugio], that [former] in most [cases] I embrace of my own accord [ultroneus]. If something drives another before itself [ante se prae agit], I would believe it to impress an equal motion: for I see that what is carried by the hand is as it were one with the hand itself, and is moved through an-[p. 227]other [per aliud]. Certainly, if sense is to be consulted, in a ship driven forth evenly [aequaliter] to the horizon with a course however most swift, we feel the wind more than the motion of the ship.

Quae autem commemoras exempla, quis concedet, ex prius impresso impetu contingere magis, quam ex praesenti? Certe si currus impingat in primo passu, tantumdem fit quam si in medio itinere. Et idem est de navicula & equo. Ad hoc conferet motus prior, ut impactio sit gravior, unde & vehementiorem in nobis sortiatur effectum. Sed ulterius quis respondeat? Qui e navi vel curru desiliunt, num sentiunt se motu currus vel navis inclinari? Si caderet aliquid de malo navis in manum stantis in littore, eundem sensum facit quem faceret in vectoris manum. Qui cursu iactum proritant, manifestum est prius semetipsos sistere quam ipsum iactum dent; saltus autem ipsius corporis motus est, quem accendi paulatim congruum est.

But the examples which you mention, who will grant that they happen more from an impetus previously impressed than from a present [one]? Certainly, if a chariot strikes at the first step, just as much happens as if in the middle of the journey. And the same is [true] of the little boat and the horse. To this the prior motion will contribute: that the collision [impactio] be heavier, whence also it obtains [sortiatur] a more vehement effect in us. But who would answer further? Those who leap down from a ship or chariot, do they feel themselves inclined by the motion of the chariot or ship? If something were to fall from the mast of a ship into the hand of one standing on the shore, it makes the same sensation which it would make on [in] the hand of a passenger [vectoris]. Those who provoke [proritant] a throw with a run, it is manifest that they stop themselves before they give the throw itself; but a leap is a motion of the body itself, which it is congruous should be kindled little by little.

Quod etiam de malleis fabrorum & in universum de gravioribus maiorem ictum facientibus ais, clara quidem res est, sed plures fortassis eiusdem effectus causae promittuntur. Nam & graviora seu maiora eiusdem densitatis velocius feruntur; & quoniam densitate agitur, maiora autem semper plures partes suae naturae habent, & a pluribus partibus plures etiam effecti partes nascuntur; confectum [p. 228] est maiores esse debere pulsus, sive impetum intrinsecus concipiat, sive non; pulsus enim maior non ex solo impetu; sed etiam ex partibus ipsius gravis ex parte nascitur.

What you say also about the hammers of the smiths, and in general [in universum] about heavier things making a greater blow, is indeed a clear matter, but perhaps several causes of the same effect are put forward [promittuntur]. For both heavier or greater things of the same density are borne more swiftly; and since it is done [agitur] by density, and greater things always have more parts of their nature, and from more parts more parts of the effect are also born; it is concluded [confectum [p. 228] est] that the drivings [pulsus] must be greater, whether [the body] conceives impetus intrinsically or not; for a greater driving is born not from impetus alone, but also in part [ex parte] from the parts of the heavy thing [gravis] itself.

Addo exemplum quod ipsam rem conficiet, si de veritate ipsius constet. Aiunt Venetiis comparuisse ante aliquot annos circumforaneum natione Turcam, cuius haec ars erat. Ex summo Turris sancti Marci, suspendi se faciebat in hemicyclio, stantem an sedentem non memini, & fune coram toto populo secto, decidebat in pavimentum sine nocumento. In certa quippe a terra distantia hemicyclio exibat ipse intactus, cum hemicyclium in mille diffringeretur particulas: hoc si verum est (pro quo tuam fidem imploro, Andabata) quid superest quod responderi possit cum videas impetum egressu ex hemicyclio elusum, ne quid in vectorem posset cum navigium assulatim dispareret.

I add an example which will settle [conficiet] the matter itself, if it be established [constet] about its truth. They say that at Venice some years ago there appeared a mountebank [circumforaneum], by nation a Turk, whose art was this. From the top of the Tower of Saint Mark he had himself suspended in a half-hoop [hemicyclio], standing or sitting I do not remember, and, the rope being cut before the whole people, he fell down onto the pavement without harm. For at a certain distance from the earth [terra] he went out of the half-hoop himself untouched, while the half-hoop was shattered into a thousand little particles: if this is true (for which I implore your faith [fidem], Andabata), what remains which could be replied, since you see the impetus eluded by the going-out from the half-hoop, so that it could do nothing against [in] the one carried [vectorem], while the vessel [navigium] was vanishing [dispareret] in splinters [assulatim]?
Andab. De veritate vos videritis: hoc assero, virum probum utrique vestrum notum mihi confirmavisse suis ipsum oculis factum vidisse.

Andab. About the truth you will see [videritis] for yourselves: this I assert, that an honest man [virum probum] known to each of you confirmed to me that he himself had seen it done with his own eyes.
Asphal. Neque ego quicquam regero, nisi me non esse tentandi avidum.
Asphal. Nor do I retort [regero] anything, except that I am not eager to try [it].

Ereu. At cum libuerit, sic experitor, in doliolum {?immitte} saxum quod casu nosti diruptum iri; fac dolium ita in itinere impingere, [p. 229] ut emittat saxum non longe a terra, & alieno periculo tutus eventum aspicies.

Ereu. But when it shall please [you], make trial [experitor] thus: put [{?immitte}] into a little cask [doliolum] a stone which you know would be burst [diruptum iri] by a fall; make the cask so strike on its way [p. 229] that it sends out the stone not far from the earth, and, safe at another’s peril, you will look upon the outcome.
Asphal. Dedo me, atque proinde nisi Andabatae quicquam paret, secundam obiectionem hac nihilo leviorem & plenam subtilissimis speculationibus propono.
Asphal. I surrender [Dedo me], and accordingly, unless anything is apparent [paret] to Andabata, I propose a second objection, in nothing lighter than this, and full of most subtle speculations.
Andab. Audire aveo, bonis itaque propone avibus.
Andab. I long to hear; propose [it], then, with good birds [bonis avibus].

Asphal. Itaque talis est ex Ptolomaeo argumentatio: Motus circularis hanc habet naturam ut reiiciat procul centro, quae circumferentiae sunt applicita. Tantus itaque telluris motus castra, arbores, montes in coelum eiaculabitur. Galilaeus admisso experimento subtilissime demonstrat ex proportione tangentium & secantium nihil a tellure reiectum iri.

Asphal. Thus, then, is the argumentation from Ptolemy: Circular motion has this nature, that it throws back [reiiciat] far from the centre the things which are applied to the circumference. So great a motion of the earth [telluris], therefore, will hurl camps, trees, mountains into heaven. Galileo, the experiment being admitted, most subtly demonstrates from the proportion of tangents and secants that nothing will be thrown off [reiectum iri] from the earth [tellure].

terms: arbor = tree, beam; malus = mast (vs. malum = evil, apple).
The ship’s-mast experiment (Galileo, Dialogo II): a weight dropped from the mast of a moving ship; White doubts the experiment can be cleanly performed (wind, unsteady mast).
supine: hard to take / to carry out / to comprehend.
Here probably ‘hard to bring off in practice’ as well as to judge.
impressed force; quality impressed by a mover.
Late-scholastic impetus theory (Buridan); Galileo’s frictionless plane keeps impetus ‘in aeternum’; White, like Simplicio, rejects an impressed quality that outlasts its cause.
I savour not a whit more than Simplicio
sapere = taste, relish; understand, be wise about.
Ironic: White sides with Galileo’s Aristotelian interlocutor in rejecting the ‘impressed quality’.
‘out of the way’ (tollere e medio = remove) and ‘from the medium’.
Pun: removing every impediment ‘e medio’ = removing the medium itself, which for White limits all motion.
White: the medium’s resistance fixes the determinate speed/extent of motion; inward vs. surface limitation.
No motion without a cause actually present — White’s anti-impetus principle.
Rare sense; Ereunius complains Andabata has thrown him off course.
motion shared by container and contained (ship and passenger, earth and bodies).
Classical-military term (Hero of Alexandria) used for a crossbow.
tube … by force of nitre powder
Galileo, Dialogo II: fowlers shoot birds in flight by turning the gun with them.
offspring … to a parent not its own
misattributing an effect to the wrong cause.
The ‘Parthian shot’ fired while fleeing; White argues no difference of range is reported.
Naval gunnery: commanders aim by position (situm), not by allowance for the ship’s motion.
the hammers of the smiths … musical harmony
Legend of Pythagoras discovering consonances from smiths’ hammers of unequal weights (Nicomachus, Boethius, Macrobius).
to the point; appropriately; from the facts.
Ereunius plays on ex re … ex re ipsa.
being carried; carrier or carried person.
Key distinction: motion present by being carried vs. impetus surviving its cause.
moved by something else, per accidens.
Aristotelian: what is carried in the hand is moved per aliud, not by an impressed impetus.
Consistent with glossary rendering; here the impact of a hammer.
it is made up / settled / proved.
Logical sense of conficere (also ‘conficiet’ = will settle).
Anecdote of a Turkish acrobat at St Mark’s, Venice; not otherwise identified here.
Apparatus in which the Turk was let fall; exact form unclear.
disparere (late Latin: disappear); possibly misprint for dispereret (‘perish’).
Either way: the carriage was destroyed while its rider escaped its impetus.
perfect subjunctive/future perfect: ‘that is your affair’.
Roman augury; pun on the birds shot in flight above.
Ptolemy, Almagest I.7: a rotating earth would fling off bodies; Galileo, Dialogo II, answers by the ratio of tangent to secant (fall-back from the tangent is infinitesimal).
pareo = appear, be evident; or obey.
Asphalius defers to Andabata if he has anything further.
